claims.source: In the lamina, L3 neurons display a unique dendritic projection pattern in which all dendrites project to one side of the neurite (Figure 2M). Dendritic processes were largely normal in dFezf null neurons (compare Figure 2M and N).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological observations shown in Figure 2M and N.

claims.claim: Disrupting dFezf did not cause an obvious change in L3 cell fate.
claims.source: In addition, the mutant L3 neurons did not express transcription factors specific to other lamina neurons (Figure 2O–Q) and still expressed L3-specific markers early in development (see Figure 3), showing that disrupting dFezf did not cause an obvious change in cell fate.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2O-Q and Figure 3.

claims.claim: Some L3-specific genes are downregulated in dFezf1 L3 neurons.
claims.source: However, some L3-specific genes are downregulated in dFezf1 L3 neurons, and genes expressed in other lamina neurons become upregulated (see below).
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data presented later in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Genes expressed in other lamina neurons become upregulated in dFezf1 L3 neurons.
claims.source: However, some L3-specific genes are downregulated in dFezf1 L3 neurons, and genes expressed in other lamina neurons become upregulated (see below).
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data presented later in the manuscript.

claims.claim: dFezf is cell autonomously required for proper axon terminal morphology and layer specificity.
claims.source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that dFezf is cell autonomously required for proper axon terminal morphology and layer specificity, yet dispensable for dendrite formation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MARCM experiments showing cell-autonomous effects.

claims.claim: dFezf is dispensable for dendrite formation.
claims.source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that dFezf is cell autonomously required for proper axon terminal morphology and layer specificity, yet dispensable for dendrite formation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that dendrites are normal in dFezf mutants.

claims.claim: At 24 hr APF, the axons of wild type L3 neurons terminate in the proximal domain of the outer medulla directly above R7 growth cones.
claims.source: In early pupal development (~24 hr APF), the axons of wild type L3 neurons terminate in the proximal domain of the outer medulla directly above R7 growth cones (Figure 3A,B,E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3A,B,E.

claims.claim: The axons of dFezf1 neurons incorrectly terminated within the distal domain of the outer medulla at 24 hr APF.
claims.source: The axons of dFezf1 neurons incorrectly terminated within the distal domain of the outer medulla (Figure 3C–E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3C-E.

claims.claim: dFezf1 L3 growth cones terminated just underneath the growth cones of R8 photoreceptors at 24 hr APF.
claims.source: Under these conditions L3 growth cones terminated just underneath the growth cones of R8 photoreceptors (Figure 3C), and occasionally terminated slightly more distally so that they completely overlapped with R8 growth cones (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claims.claim: By mid-pupal development (~48 hr APF), the growth cones of wild type L3 neurons have segregated into the developing M3 layer.
claims.source: By mid-pupal development (~48 hr APF), the growth cones of wild type L3 neurons have segregated into the developing M3 layer (Figure 3F,G,K).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3F,G,K.

claims.claim: All of the growth cones of dFezf1 L3 neurons displayed abnormal morphologies, defects in layer specificity, or both at 48 hr APF.
claims.source: However, we found that all of the growth cones of dFezf1 L3 neurons displayed abnormal morphologies, defects in layer specificity, or both.
claims.evidence: This is based on morphological observations at 48 hr APF.

claims.claim: 67% of abnormal dFezf1 L3 growth cones exclusively innervated the developing M1 and M2 layers at 48 hr APF.
claims.source: Most of the abnormal growth cones (67%) exclusively innervated the developing M1 and M2 layers (Figure 3H,K).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3K and images in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: 33% of dFezf1 L3 growth cones terminated in the developing M3 layer or in more proximal layers (e.g. M4-M6) at 48 hr APF.
claims.source: The remaining 33% of the growth cones terminated in the developing M3 layer (Figure 3I,K) or in more proximal layers (e.g. M4-M6) (Figure 3J,K).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3K and images in Figure 3I,J.

claims.claim: dFezf1 L3 growth cones that terminated in M3 or more proximal layers also displayed abnormal swellings in distal layers (i.e. the developing M1 and M2 layers) at 48 hr APF.
claims.source: However, each of these growth cones also displayed abnormal swellings in distal layers (i.e. the developing M1 and M2 layers) (Figure 3I,J, arrowheads).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3I,J.

claims.claim: Defects in morphology and layer innervation at 48 hr APF are consistent with the abnormalities observed in adult flies.
claims.source: These defects in morphology and layer innervation are consistent with the abnormalities observed in adult flies under these conditions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing developmental and adult phenotypes.

claims.claim: Similar deficits in L3 growth cone targeting were observed in MARCM experiments using the dFezf2 mutant allele.
claims.source: We observed similar deficits in L3 growth cone targeting in MARCM experiments when we used a different dFezf mutant allele (dFezf2) that eliminates the entire dFezf open reading frame (Weng et al., 2010) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citation to Weng et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Defects in growth cone targeting during pupal development and abnormal layer innervation in adult flies caused by dFezf1 or dFezf2 were completely rescued by a single copy of a BAC containing the dFezf locus.
claims.source: Moreover, defects in growth cone targeting during pupal development, as well as abnormal layer innervation in adult flies caused by dFezf1 or dFezf2 were completely rescued by a single copy of a bacterial artificial chromosome (BAC) containing the dFezf locus (Figure 3L,M, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3L,M and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: dFezf is cell-autonomously required for the targeting of L3 growth cones to the proximal domain of the outer medulla.
claims.source: Together, these findings demonstrate that dFezf is cell-autonomously required for the targeting of L3 growth cones to the proximal domain of the outer medulla, which may be necessary for the subsequent segregation of the growth cones into the developing M3 layer.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MARCM experiments and rescue experiments.

claims.claim: Targeting to the proximal domain of the outer medulla may be necessary for the subsequent segregation of L3 growth cones into the developing M3 layer.
claims.source: Together, these findings demonstrate that dFezf is cell-autonomously required for the targeting of L3 growth cones to the proximal domain of the outer medulla, which may be necessary for the subsequent segregation of the growth cones into the developing M3 layer.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the developmental observations.

claims.claim: The large majority of the nascent dFezf1 clones (82%) terminated within the distal domain of the outer medulla.
claims.source: Unlike the youngest wild type clones, the large majority of the nascent dFezf1 clones (82%) terminated within the distal domain of the outer medulla similar to their older counter parts (Figure 3E,N,O), consistent with most of these neurons directly innervating this region.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3E and images in Figure 3N,O.

claims.claim: CadN and Sema-1a function synergistically to restrict L3 growth cones to the outer medulla during pupal development, preventing innervation of the serpentine layer and inner medulla.
claims.source: CadN and Sema-1a function synergistically to restrict L3 growth cones to the outer medulla during pupal development, preventing innervation of the serpentine layer and inner medulla (Pecot et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pecot et al., 2013.

claims.claim: L3 neurons lacking the function of dFezf, CadN and Sema-1a predominantly innervated the distal domain of the outer medulla in early pupal development.
claims.source: MARCM experiments revealed the latter to be correct. L3 neurons lacking the function of dFezf, CadN and Sema-1a predominantly innervated the distal domain of the outer medulla in early pupal development (Figure 3E,P), similar to L3 neurons lacking dFezf function only (Figure 3C–E), although the triple KO neurons more frequently terminated within the R8 growth cone layer.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3E and images in Figure 3P.

claims.claim: The triple KO neurons (dFezf, CadN, Sema-1a) did not mis-target beyond the outer medulla like CadN/Sema-1a double mutant L3 neurons.
claims.source: Importantly, the triple KO neurons did not mis-target beyond the outer medulla like CadN/Sema-1a double mutant L3 neurons (Figure 3Q,R).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3R and images in Figure 3Q.

claims.claim: L3 neurons lacking dFezf function directly innervate the distal domain of the outer medulla.
claims.source: Combined with our analyses of newly born dFezf1 L3 neurons, these data suggest that L3 neurons lacking dFezf function directly innervate the distal domain of the outer medulla, which is consistent with a switch in broad domain specificity.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic experiments with youngest clones and triple mutants.

claims.claim: Mis-expressing dFezf in L5 neurons using 6–60 GAL4 had no effect on L5 growth cone position in early pupal development.
claims.source: We found that the expression of dFezf-HA had no effect on L5 growth cone position in early pupal development. The growth cones of dFezf-expressing L5 neurons innervated the proximal domain of the outer medulla in a manner indistinguishable from wild type neurons (Figure 4B–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4D and images in Figure 4B,C.

claims.claim: dFezf expression did not affect the layer position or morphology of L5 terminals in adult flies.
claims.source: DFezf expression did not affect the layer position or morphology of L5 terminals, but caused defects in the distal arborizations of the vast majority of L5 neurons (Figure 4F–H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4H and images in Figure 4F,G.

claims.claim: 82% of L5 neurons mis-expressing dFezf displayed reduced distal arborizations that failed to extend into the M2 layer.
claims.source: 82% of L5 neurons mis-expressing dFezf displayed reduced distal arborizations that failed to extend into the M2 layer (Figure 4F,H), and 15% of neurons extended distal branches into neighboring columns (Figure 4G,H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4H and images in Figure 4F,G.

claims.claim: dFezf function may antagonize innervation of the distal outer medulla.
claims.source: These findings, along with the fact that dFezf null L3 neurons inappropriately arborize in distal medulla layers, suggests that dFezf function may antagonize innervation of the distal outer medulla.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mis-expression experiments in L5 and the loss-of-function phenotype in L3.

claims.claim: All L2 neurons mis-expressing dFezf-HA inappropriately terminated within the proximal domain of the outer medulla in early pupal development.
claims.source: Using this criteria we found that, in early pupal development, the growth cones of all L2 neurons mis-expressing dFezf-HA inappropriately terminated within the proximal domain of the outer medulla (Figure 4J–L), and in adult flies the large majority of these neurons (88%) incorrectly innervated the M3 layer (Figure 4M–O).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4L and images in Figure 4J,K.

claims.claim: 88% of L2 neurons mis-expressing dFezf-HA incorrectly innervated the M3 layer in adult flies.
claims.source: Using this criteria we found that, in early pupal development, the growth cones of all L2 neurons mis-expressing dFezf-HA inappropriately terminated within the proximal domain of the outer medulla (Figure 4J–L), and in adult flies the large majority of these neurons (88%) incorrectly innervated the M3 layer (Figure 4M–O).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4O and images in Figure 4M,N.

claims.claim: dFezf-HA expressing L2 neurons still displayed terminal-like swellings within the M2 layer, indicating a partial rather than complete change in layer specificity.
claims.source: In all cases dFezf-HA expressing L2 neurons still displayed terminal-like swellings within the M2 layer, indicating a partial rather than complete change in layer specificity.
claims.evidence: This is based on morphological observations in the mis-expression experiments.

claims.claim: Mis-expressing dFezf in L2 neurons is sufficient to induce innervation of the proximal domain of the outer medulla.
claims.source: These experiments demonstrate that mis-expressing dFezf in L2 neurons is sufficient to induce innervation of the proximal domain of the outer medulla, and cause ectopic innervation of the L3 target layer M3.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the L2 mis-expression experiments.

claims.claim: Mis-expressing dFezf in L2 neurons causes ectopic innervation of the L3 target layer M3.
claims.source: These experiments demonstrate that mis-expressing dFezf in L2 neurons is sufficient to induce innervation of the proximal domain of the outer medulla, and cause ectopic innervation of the L3 target layer M3.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the L2 mis-expression experiments.

claims.claim: dFezf acts instructively to direct growth cone targeting.
claims.source: Collectively, our mis-expression studies in L2 and L5 neurons support that dFezf acts instructively to direct growth cone targeting.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined mis-expression experiments in L2 and L5.

claims.claim: dFezf achieves growth cone targeting by antagonizing innervation of the distal outer medulla and promoting innervation of the proximal outer medulla.
claims.source: We hypothesize that dFezf achieves this by antagonizing innervation of the distal outer medulla and promoting innervation of the proximal outer medulla (see discussion).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the combined loss-of-function and mis-expression data.

claims.claim: 455 differentially expressed (DE) genes (padj <0.05) were identified between wild type and dFezf mutant L3 neurons at 40 hr APF.
claims.source: Differential expression analysis identified 455 differentially expressed (DE) genes (padj <0.05) (Figure 5C, and Supplementary file 3), and changes in the expression of several of these were verified at the protein level (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C and Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: 110 of the 455 DE genes are cell surface and secreted genes.
claims.source: Using previously curated databases (Kurusu et al., 2008; Tan et al., 2015), we found that 110 of the 455 DE genes are cell surface and secreted genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), consistent with a role for dFezf in regulating cell-cell communication.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of RNA-seq data using curated databases, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Large fractions of DE genes were up or downregulated (190 and 265 genes, respectively).
claims.source: Large fractions of DE genes were up or downregulated (190 and 265 genes, respectively) (see Figure 5C and Supplementary file 2), indicating that dFezf function serves to both activate and repress gene expression, either directly or through intermediate regulators.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C and Supplementary file 2.

claims.claim: dFezf function serves to both activate and repress gene expression, either directly or through intermediate regulators.
claims.source: Large fractions of DE genes were up or downregulated (190 and 265 genes, respectively) (see Figure 5C and Supplementary file 2), indicating that dFezf function serves to both activate and repress gene expression, either directly or through intermediate regulators.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that genes are both up and downregulated in the mutant.

claims.claim: The top three most significant DE genes are dprs 17, 13, and 1, respectively.
claims.source: However, ranking the DE genes based on significance revealed several intriguing candidates. For example, using this criteria, the top three genes are dprs 17, 13, and 1, respectively, which are members of the dpr cell surface family (Nakamura et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: The mRNA levels of dprs 17, 13, and 1 change more than 1000 fold when dFezf is disrupted in L3 neurons.
claims.source: The mRNA levels of all three genes change more than 1000 fold when dFezf is disrupted in L3 neurons (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Dpr 17 is exclusively expressed in L3 neurons in the lamina.
claims.source: Dpr 17 is exclusively expressed in L3 neurons in the lamina and dpr1 is expressed in L3 and L4 neurons (Tan et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tan et al., 2015.

claims.claim: dpr1 is expressed in L3 and L4 neurons.
claims.source: Dpr 17 is exclusively expressed in L3 neurons in the lamina and dpr1 is expressed in L3 and L4 neurons (Tan et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tan et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Dpr17 and dpr1 are downregulated in the absence of dFezf function.
claims.source: Both are downregulated in the absence of dFezf function, and for dpr17 we confirmed this at the protein level (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B').
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data and protein expression data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B'.

claims.claim: Dpr13 is highly expressed in L2 neurons and moderately expressed in L4 neurons.
claims.source: Dpr13 is highly expressed in L2 neurons and moderately expressed in L4 neurons (Tan et al., 2015), and is upregulated in dFezf null L3 neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tan et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Dpr13 is upregulated in dFezf null L3 neurons.
claims.source: Dpr13 is highly expressed in L2 neurons and moderately expressed in L4 neurons (Tan et al., 2015), and is upregulated in dFezf null L3 neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Eight other dpr genes are differentially expressed between wild type and dFezf null L3 neurons.
claims.source: In addition to these, eight other dpr genes are differentially expressed between wild type and dFezf null L3 neurons (Figure 5D), suggesting that dpr genes are prominent direct or indirect dFezf targets.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Dpr proteins are immunoglobulin (Ig) domain containing cell surface molecules (21 dprs) that bind heterophilically to dpr interacting proteins (DIPs) (9 DIPs).
claims.source: Dpr proteins are immunoglobulin (Ig) domain containing cell surface molecules (21 dprs) that bind heterophilically to dpr interacting proteins (DIPs) (9 DIPs) (Carrillo et al., 2015; Özkan et al., 2013), which are also cell surface molecules and members of the Ig superfamily (IgSF).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Carrillo et al., 2015 and Özkan et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Dpr and DIP proteins are expressed in a matching manner between lamina neurons (including L3) and their synaptic targets in the medulla.
claims.source: Dpr and DIP proteins are expressed in a matching manner between lamina neurons (including L3) and their synaptic targets in the medulla, and specific dpr-DIP interactions, or combinations of them, have been proposed to encode synaptic specificity (Tan et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tan et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Specific dpr-DIP interactions, or combinations of them, have been proposed to encode synaptic specificity.
claims.source: Dpr and DIP proteins are expressed in a matching manner between lamina neurons (including L3) and their synaptic targets in the medulla, and specific dpr-DIP interactions, or combinations of them, have been proposed to encode synaptic specificity (Tan et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tan et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The mRNA levels of Netrin-A and B (NetA/B) were drastically reduced in dFezf null L3 neurons compared to wild type neurons at 40 hr APF.
claims.source: Our RNA-seq analyses revealed that the mRNA levels of Netrin-A and B (NetA/B) were drastically reduced in dFezf null L3 neurons compared to wild type neurons at 40 hr APF (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B.

claims.claim: dFezf non-autonomously regulates R8 layer specificity via activation of Netrin expression in L3 neurons.
claims.source: This suggested that, in addition to cell autonomously regulating L3 targeting, dFezf non-autonomously regulates R8 layer specificity via activation of Netrin expression in L3 neurons.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RNA-seq data showing reduced Netrin expression and known role of Netrin in R8 targeting.

claims.claim: NetB is expressed at much higher levels than NetA in L3 neurons.
claims.source: We focused on NetB protein because NetB is expressed at much higher levels than NetA in L3 neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B) (Tan et al., 2015), and the expression of NetB in L3 neurons is sufficient to support proper R8 layer specificity in the background of a NetA/B deletion (Timofeev et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B and citation to Tan et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The expression of NetB in L3 neurons is sufficient to support proper R8 layer specificity in the background of a NetA/B deletion.
claims.source: We focused on NetB protein because NetB is expressed at much higher levels than NetA in L3 neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B) (Tan et al., 2015), and the expression of NetB in L3 neurons is sufficient to support proper R8 layer specificity in the background of a NetA/B deletion (Timofeev et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Timofeev et al., 2012.

claims.claim: At 24 hr APF, NetB is expressed in the perinuclear region of the oldest lamina neurons (most anterior).
claims.source: At 24 hr APF we observed NetB expression in the perinuclear region of the oldest lamina neurons (most anterior) (Figure 6A–D').
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6A-D'.

claims.claim: NetB is expressed by L3, L4 and L5 neurons, but not L1 or L2 neurons at 24 hr APF.
claims.source: Using markers specific for different lamina neuron subclasses we discovered that NetB is expressed by L3, L4 and L5 neurons, but not L1 or L2 neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data using cell-type specific markers.

claims.claim: At 48 hr APF, NetB expression remained specific to L3, L4 and L5 neurons in the lamina, although it was most strongly expressed in L3 neurons at this stage.
claims.source: At 48 hr APF NetB expression remained specific to L3, L4 and L5 neurons in the lamina, although it was most strongly expressed in L3 neurons at this stage (Figure 6E–H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6E-H.

claims.claim: L3 neurons express NetB much earlier in development than when NetB immunoreactivity is first detected within the M3 layer at ~40 hr APF.
claims.source: Thus, while NetB immunoreactivity is first detected within the M3 layer at ~40 hr APF (Timofeev et al., 2012), which coincides with the segregation of L3 growth cones into the developing M3 layer, L3 neurons express NetB much earlier in development.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the timing of NetB expression in L3 cell bodies versus the M3 layer.

claims.claim: NetB is also expressed by L4 and L5 neurons during pupal development, and thus may regulate circuit assembly within multiple developing layers.
claims.source: In addition, we found that NetB is also expressed by L4 and L5 neurons during pupal development, and thus may regulate circuit assembly within multiple developing layers.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the expression pattern of NetB in multiple lamina neuron types.

claims.claim: Disrupting dFezf in single L3 neurons in MARCM experiments drastically reduced NetB immunostaining in L3 cell bodies at 48 hr APF.
claims.source: Disrupting dFezf in single L3 neurons in MARCM experiments drastically reduced NetB immunostaining in L3 cell bodies at 48 hr APF (Figure 7A–B').
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7A-B'.

claims.claim: The expression of dFezf RNAi in the lamina eliminated detectable dFezf immunoreactivity in L3 neurons.
claims.source: The expression of dFezf RNAi in the lamina eliminated detectable dFezf immunoreactivity in L3 neurons (Figure 7C,D), and considerably reduced NetB immunostaining in L3 somas and the developing M3 layer at 48 hr APF (Figure 7E,F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claims.claim: dFezf RNAi considerably reduced NetB immunostaining in L3 somas and the developing M3 layer at 48 hr APF.
claims.source: The expression of dFezf RNAi in the lamina eliminated detectable dFezf immunoreactivity in L3 neurons (Figure 7C,D), and considerably reduced NetB immunostaining in L3 somas and the developing M3 layer at 48 hr APF (Figure 7E,F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7E,F.

claims.claim: dFezf is cell autonomously required for NetB protein expression in L3 neurons.
claims.source: Together, these experiments demonstrate that dFezf is cell autonomously required for NetB protein expression in L3 neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MARCM and RNAi experiments showing loss of NetB expression.

claims.claim: While no wild type L2 neurons expressed NetB at 48 hr APF, 99% of dFezf-HA expressing L2 neurons ectopically expressed NetB.
claims.source: We found that, while no wild type L2 neurons expressed NetB at 48 hr APF (Figure 7I), 99% of dFezf-HA expressing L2 neurons ectopically expressed NetB (Figure 7J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7I,J.

claims.claim: In the context of L2 neurons, dFezf is sufficient to induce NetB expression.
claims.source: Thus, in the context of L2 neurons dFezf is sufficient to induce NetB expression.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mis-expression experiments in L2 neurons.

claims.claim: dFezf, either directly or through intermediate regulators, activates Netrin expression in L3 neurons.
claims.source: Collectively, our RNA-seq and protein expression experiments support that dFezf, either directly or through intermediate regulators, activates Netrin expression in L3 neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined RNA-seq, loss-of-function, and mis-expression data.

claims.claim: When dFezf was disrupted via RNAi, 45% of R8 axons terminated within inappropriate layers.
claims.source: Normally, R8 axons terminate in the M3 layer (Figure 7K,M). When dFezf was disrupted 45% of R8 axons terminated within inappropriate layers (Figure 7L,M).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7M and images in Figure 7K,L.

claims.claim: 29% of R8 axons terminated in layers proximal to M3 (i.e. M4-M6) when dFezf was disrupted.
claims.source: 29% of the axons terminated in layers proximal to M3 (i.e. M4-M6) and 16% terminated in distal layers (i.e. M0-M2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data.

claims.claim: 16% of R8 axons terminated in distal layers (i.e. M0-M2) when dFezf was disrupted.
claims.source: 29% of the axons terminated in layers proximal to M3 (i.e. M4-M6) and 16% terminated in distal layers (i.e. M0-M2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data.

claims.claim: dFezf in L3 neurons is required for R8 layer specificity.
claims.source: Nonetheless, our experiments show that dFezf in L3 neurons is required for R8 layer specificity.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNAi experiments showing R8 mis-targeting.

claims.claim: dFezf regulates R8 layer specificity, to a large extent, through activation of Netrin expression in L3 neurons.
claims.source: Together with previous research, these findings along with our analyses of Netrin gene and protein (NetB) expression indicate that dFezf regulates R8 layer specificity, to a large extent, through activation of Netrin expression in L3 neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined findings about dFezf regulation of Netrin and the role of Netrin in R8 targeting.

claims.claim: Within the M3 layer, L3 axons synapse onto the dendrites of transmedullary nine neurons (Tm9).
claims.source: Within the M3 layer L3 axons synapse onto the dendrites of transmedullary nine neurons (Tm9) (Gao et al., 2008; Takemura et al., 2013; Takemura et al., 2015), and synapses between R8 and Tm9 have also been reported (Gao et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gao et al., 2008; Takemura et al., 2013; and Takemura et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Synapses between R8 and Tm9 have been reported.
claims.source: Within the M3 layer L3 axons synapse onto the dendrites of transmedullary nine neurons (Tm9) (Gao et al., 2008; Takemura et al., 2013; Takemura et al., 2015), and synapses between R8 and Tm9 have also been reported (Gao et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gao et al., 2008.

claims.claim: dFezf may be required to maintain 9–9 GAL4 expression in L3 neurons.
claims.source: The decreased labeling observed in mutant clones is likely due to a reduction in 9–9 GAL4 activity during pupal development rather than cell death, as dFezf1 L3 neurons in adult flies were strongly labeled with a pan-neuronal driver (i.e. the brp locus) (see Figure 2G–I,L,N). Thus, dFezf may be required to maintain 9–9 GAL4 expression in L3 neurons.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of weak GAL4-driven labeling in mutants but strong labeling with a pan-neuronal marker.

claims.claim: Connectivity between L3 and Tm9 neurons is disrupted when dFezf is lost in L3 neurons.
claims.source: To summarize, in these experiments we did not observe overlap between the axons of dFezf null L3 neurons and Tm9 dendrites during development or in adult flies, strongly pointing to disrupted connectivity between these neurons under these conditions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of overlap between L3 axons and Tm9 dendrites in the mutant.

claims.claim: dFezf is partially required for R8-Tm9 connectivity.
claims.source: In addition, it is also likely that dFezf is partially required for R8-Tm9 connectivity, as a significant number of R8 axons terminate in layers distal to M3 in the absence of dFezf function (Figure 7L,M), and R8 axons and Tm9 dendrites are unlikely to overlap in these columns.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that R8 axons mis-target when dFezf is disrupted in L3 neurons.

claims.claim: Specific layers are built in a stepwise manner through use of transcriptional modules that cell-intrinsically instruct targeting to specific layers, and cell-extrinsically recruit other circuit components.
claims.source: Based on our findings and previous studies, we propose that specific layers are built in a stepwise manner through use of transcriptional modules that cell-intrinsically instruct targeting to specific layers, and cell-extrinsically recruit other circuit components.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the findings of the study.

claims.claim: This represents an evolutionarily conserved strategy for building laminar-specific neural circuits.
claims.source: Moreover, based on research in the mammalian nervous system we propose that this represents an evolutionarily conserved strategy for building laminar-specific neural circuits (see below).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on comparisons to mammalian systems.

claims.claim: dFezf regulates broad domain specificity in L3 neurons.
claims.source: Our findings demonstrate that dFezf regulates broad domain specificity in L3 neurons, and indicate that this step in development is crucial for L3 laminar specificity, synaptic connectivity, and for the proper assembly of the M3 layer.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the developmental and genetic experiments.

claims.claim: Broad domain specificity is crucial for L3 laminar specificity, synaptic connectivity, and for the proper assembly of the M3 layer.
claims.source: Our findings demonstrate that dFezf regulates broad domain specificity in L3 neurons, and indicate that this step in development is crucial for L3 laminar specificity, synaptic connectivity, and for the proper assembly of the M3 layer.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that disrupting broad domain targeting leads to defects in layer specificity and connectivity.

claims.claim: dFezf functions in parallel to CadN and Sema-1a in L3 neurons to regulate targeting to the proximal domain of the outer medulla.
claims.source: We show that dFezf functions in parallel to CadN and Sema-1a in L3 neurons to regulate targeting to the proximal domain of the outer medulla.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic experiments showing that dFezf and CadN/Sema-1a have distinct effects.

claims.claim: CadN and Sema-1a mRNA levels in wild type and dFezf mutant L3 neurons were not significantly different at 40 hr APF.
claims.source: However, CadN and Sema-1a mRNA levels in wild type and dFezf mutant L3 neurons were not significantly different (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B), demonstrating that dFezf is not necessary for their expression at 40 hr APF.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B.

claims.claim: dFezf is not necessary for CadN and Sema-1a expression at 40 hr APF.
claims.source: However, CadN and Sema-1a mRNA levels in wild type and dFezf mutant L3 neurons were not significantly different (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B), demonstrating that dFezf is not necessary for their expression at 40 hr APF.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: CadN and Sema-1a double mutant L3 neurons display defects in dendrite morphology.
claims.source: In line with this, CadN and Sema-1a double mutant L3 neurons display defects in dendrite morphology (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C), but dendrites were qualitatively normal in the absence of dFezf function (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C), indicating that disrupting dFezf does not affect CadN and Sema-1a function.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C.

claims.claim: Dendrites were qualitatively normal in the absence of dFezf function.
claims.source: In line with this, CadN and Sema-1a double mutant L3 neurons display defects in dendrite morphology (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C), but dendrites were qualitatively normal in the absence of dFezf function (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C), indicating that disrupting dFezf does not affect CadN and Sema-1a function.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C.

claims.claim: Disrupting dFezf does not affect CadN and Sema-1a function.
claims.source: In line with this, CadN and Sema-1a double mutant L3 neurons display defects in dendrite morphology (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C), but dendrites were qualitatively normal in the absence of dFezf function (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C), indicating that disrupting dFezf does not affect CadN and Sema-1a function.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that dendrites are normal in dFezf mutants but not in CadN/Sema-1a mutants.

claims.claim: dFezf acts in parallel to CadN and Sema-1a to regulate L3 growth cone targeting within the outer medulla.
claims.source: Together, these data strongly support that dFezf acts in parallel to CadN and Sema-1a to regulate L3 growth cone targeting within the outer medulla (see discussion).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined genetic and expression data.

claims.claim: In the mouse IPL, Fezf1 is expressed in a subset of bipolar cells that innervate specific sublaminae (i.e. layers).
claims.source: For instance, in the inner plexiform layer of the mouse retina, which is analogous to the medulla in structure and function (Sanes and Zipursky, 2010), Fezf1 is expressed in a subset of bipolar cells that innervate specific sublaminae (i.e. layers) (Shekhar et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sanes and Zipursky, 2010 and Shekhar et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Fezf1 in specific types of bipolar cells functions analogously to dFezf in L3 to coordinate laminar-specific connectivity.
claims.source: Bipolar cells are analogous to lamina neurons, and we hypothesize that Fezf1 in specific types of bipolar cells functions analogously to dFezf in L3 to coordinate laminar-specific connectivity.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the analogous expression patterns and circuit organization.

claims.claim: In the cerebral cortex of mice, Fezf2 cell-intrinsically controls the identity of subcortically projecting pyramidal neurons that predominantly reside in layer V.
claims.source: In the cerebral cortex of mice, Fezf2 cell-intrinsically controls the identity of subcortically projecting pyramidal neurons that predominantly reside in layer V (Chen et al., 2005a; Chen et al., 2005b; Molyneaux et al., 2005), and pyramidal neuron identity was shown to be important for the laminar positioning of specific classes of GABAergic neurons (Lodato et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2005a; Chen et al., 2005b; Molyneaux et al., 2005; and Lodato et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Pyramidal neuron identity was shown to be important for the laminar positioning of specific classes of GABAergic neurons.
claims.source: In the cerebral cortex of mice, Fezf2 cell-intrinsically controls the identity of subcortically projecting pyramidal neurons that predominantly reside in layer V (Chen et al., 2005a; Chen et al., 2005b; Molyneaux et al., 2005), and pyramidal neuron identity was shown to be important for the laminar positioning of specific classes of GABAergic neurons (Lodato et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lodato et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Fezf2 in the cortex may organize laminar-specific circuitry through cell-intrinsic and cell-extrinsic mechanisms similar to dFezf in the medulla.
claims.source: While it remains unclear as to whether Fezf2 in pyramidal cells regulates the expression of molecules that act non-autonomously to recruit specific inhibitory neurons (analogous to Netrin), one interesting possibility is that Fezf2 in the cortex organizes laminar-specific circuitry through cell-intrinsic and cell-extrinsic mechanisms similar to dFezf in the medulla.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the findings in Drosophila and known functions of Fezf2 in mice.

results.result: dFezf is expressed selectively in L3 neurons from early pupal stages (at least 12 hr APF) through adulthood, but not in late third instar larvae or other lamina cell types. This temporal and spatial expression pattern is consistent with dFezf playing an important role in L3 development.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33 provide direct immunostaining evidence across developmental stages showing selective L3 expression. C34 appropriately interprets this pattern as consistent with a developmental role. The data are clear and the inference is reasonable.

results.result: dFezf is cell-autonomously required for proper L3 axon terminal morphology and layer specificity in adult flies. In dFezf mutants, 84% of L3 axons terminate inappropriately in distal layers (M1-M2) with abnormal terminal morphology and presynaptic markers, while dendrites remain normal and cell fate is not obviously altered.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C42 provide quantitative MARCM data with appropriate controls showing specific axon targeting defects without dendrite or cell fate changes. C45-C46 appropriately conclude cell-autonomous requirement. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=383 wild type, n=260 mutant) and phenotype penetrance is high.

results.result: dFezf is cell-autonomously required for targeting L3 growth cones to the proximal domain of the outer medulla during early pupal development (24 hr APF). Loss of dFezf causes growth cones to mis-target to the distal domain, and this defect persists through mid-pupal development (48 hr APF) and is rescued by a BAC containing the dFezf locus.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C57 provide developmental time-course data showing early targeting defects that persist, with independent confirmation using a second allele (C56) and complete rescue (C57). The data demonstrate cell-autonomous requirement for broad domain targeting. Multiple time points and genetic controls strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: L3 neurons lacking dFezf function directly innervate the distal domain of the outer medulla rather than initially targeting correctly and then retracting. This is supported by analysis of newly born clones and triple mutant experiments with CadN and Sema-1a, which show that loss of dFezf prevents mis-targeting beyond the outer medulla.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63 provide two independent lines of evidence (youngest clones and epistasis with CadN/Sema-1a) supporting direct mis-targeting rather than retraction. The triple mutant logic is sound: if dFezf mutants initially target correctly, removing CadN/Sema-1a should cause deeper mis-targeting, but this is not observed. C64 appropriately concludes direct innervation.

results.result: Mis-expressing dFezf in L5 neurons (which normally target to the proximal domain) does not affect growth cone position in early development but causes defects in distal arborizations in adults, with 82% showing reduced branching into M2. This suggests dFezf may antagonize innervation of the distal outer medulla.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 provide clear quantitative data from mis-expression experiments. C68 appropriately infers antagonism of distal innervation based on both the L5 mis-expression phenotype and the L3 loss-of-function phenotype. The inference is reasonable though additional experiments would strengthen the mechanistic claim.

results.result: Mis-expressing dFezf in L2 neurons (which normally target to the distal domain) is sufficient to redirect growth cones to the proximal domain in early development and cause ectopic innervation of the M3 layer in adults (88% of neurons). This demonstrates that dFezf acts instructively to direct growth cone targeting.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C73 provide strong gain-of-function evidence with appropriate controls and quantification. The partial phenotype (C71) is acknowledged. C74 appropriately concludes instructive function based on combined L2 and L5 mis-expression data. The logic is sound: redirecting L2 from distal to proximal demonstrates instructive rather than merely permissive function.

results.result: dFezf achieves growth cone targeting by antagonizing innervation of the distal outer medulla and promoting innervation of the proximal outer medulla.
results.evaluation: C75 proposes a dual mechanism but is explicitly labeled as a hypothesis. While consistent with the loss-of-function and gain-of-function data, direct evidence for both antagonism and promotion is incomplete. The claim requires additional molecular and functional experiments to distinguish between these mechanisms.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis identified 455 differentially expressed genes (padj <0.05) between wild type and dFezf mutant L3 neurons at 40 hr APF, including 110 cell surface and secreted genes. Large fractions were upregulated (190) or downregulated (265), indicating dFezf both activates and represses gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 provide clear RNA-seq results with appropriate statistical thresholds and biological categorization. C79 appropriately infers dual regulatory function from bidirectional expression changes. Five biological replicates per condition and protein-level validation of select genes (referenced) support data quality.

results.result: The top three most significant differentially expressed genes are dpr family members (dprs 17, 13, and 1), with >1000-fold expression changes. Eight additional dpr genes are differentially expressed. Dpr proteins are cell surface molecules that bind DIPs and have been proposed to encode synaptic specificity through matching expression patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C87 provide specific RNA-seq results for dpr genes with dramatic fold-changes and appropriate citations for expression patterns. C88-C90 provide established knowledge about dpr-DIP interactions with proper citations. The data identify dprs as prominent dFezf targets, though their functional role in targeting remains to be tested.

results.result: Members of the dpr cell surface gene family are prominent direct or indirect dFezf targets, and dFezf may regulate growth cone targeting by controlling dpr expression to mediate interactions with target cells in the medulla.
results.evaluation: C24 is supported by RNA-seq data showing differential dpr expression. However, C25 is explicitly speculative ('we propose') and lacks functional validation. While dprs are strong candidates based on expression changes and known functions, direct evidence linking specific dprs to the targeting phenotype is absent.

results.result: Netrin-A and B mRNA levels are drastically reduced in dFezf null L3 neurons at 40 hr APF, suggesting dFezf non-autonomously regulates R8 layer specificity via Netrin activation. NetB is expressed at much higher levels than NetA in L3 neurons and is sufficient for R8 layer specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C91 and C93 provide RNA-seq data showing reduced Netrin expression. C92 appropriately infers non-autonomous regulation based on known Netrin function in R8 targeting (cited). C94 provides supporting citation for NetB sufficiency. The inference is well-supported by combining new expression data with established functional knowledge.

results.result: NetB protein is expressed in L3, L4, and L5 neurons (but not L1 or L2) starting at 24 hr APF, earlier than its detection in the M3 layer (~40 hr APF). This suggests NetB may regulate circuit assembly in multiple developing layers.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 provide direct immunostaining evidence for NetB expression pattern using cell-type specific markers. C98 appropriately notes the temporal discrepancy between soma and layer expression. C99 is appropriately speculative about broader function. The data clearly establish NetB expression pattern in multiple lamina neuron types.

results.result: dFezf is cell-autonomously required for NetB protein expression in L3 neurons. Disrupting dFezf in single L3 neurons (MARCM) or broadly via RNAi drastically reduces NetB immunostaining in L3 cell bodies and the developing M3 layer at 48 hr APF.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C102 provide complementary loss-of-function evidence using both single-cell (MARCM) and population-level (RNAi) approaches, with clear immunostaining data. C103 appropriately concludes cell-autonomous requirement. The dual approach strengthens the conclusion by ruling out indirect effects.

results.result: dFezf is sufficient to induce NetB expression in L2 neurons, where it is not normally expressed. In mis-expression experiments, 99% of dFezf-expressing L2 neurons ectopically expressed NetB at 48 hr APF. This demonstrates that dFezf, directly or through intermediates, activates Netrin expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C105 provide strong gain-of-function evidence with high penetrance (99%) and appropriate controls. C106 appropriately concludes activation while acknowledging uncertainty about direct versus indirect regulation. The combined loss-of-function and gain-of-function data strongly support dFezf regulation of Netrin.

results.result: dFezf in L3 neurons is required for R8 layer specificity. When dFezf is disrupted via RNAi, 45% of R8 axons terminate in inappropriate layers (29% proximal, 16% distal to M3). This demonstrates that dFezf regulates R8 layer specificity largely through activation of Netrin expression in L3 neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C109 provide quantitative data on R8 mis-targeting with adequate sample size (n=942 control, n=528 RNAi). C110-C111 appropriately conclude non-autonomous requirement and link to Netrin based on prior work. The penetrance (45%) is similar to published Netrin mutants, supporting the mechanistic link, though the proximal mis-targeting (29%) differs from prior reports and may suggest additional factors.

results.result: Within the M3 layer, L3 axons synapse onto Tm9 dendrites, and R8-Tm9 synapses have also been reported. When dFezf is lost in L3 neurons, connectivity between L3 and Tm9 is disrupted, and dFezf is likely partially required for R8-Tm9 connectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C113 establish known connectivity with appropriate citations. C122 is supported by the observation that L3 axons and Tm9 dendrites do not overlap in dFezf mutants during development or in adults. C123 is a reasonable inference based on R8 mis-targeting data. The lack of overlap strongly suggests disrupted connectivity, though direct synaptic analysis would be definitive.

results.result: dFezf may be required to maintain 9-9 GAL4 expression in L3 neurons, as mutant clones show weak GAL4-driven labeling but strong labeling with a pan-neuronal driver.
results.evaluation: C121 provides a reasonable explanation for weak labeling in mutants based on differential labeling with GAL4 versus pan-neuronal drivers, ruling out cell death. This is an appropriate technical consideration that affects interpretation of some experiments but does not undermine the main conclusions.

results.result: dFezf regulates broad domain specificity in L3 neurons, and this step is crucial for L3 laminar specificity, synaptic connectivity, and proper assembly of the M3 layer.
results.evaluation: C126 is supported by the developmental data showing dFezf controls proximal versus distal domain targeting. C127 appropriately infers importance based on the cascade of defects (layer specificity, R8 targeting, Tm9 connectivity) that result from disrupting broad domain targeting. The inference is well-supported by the comprehensive phenotypic analysis.

results.result: dFezf functions in parallel to CadN and Sema-1a to regulate L3 growth cone targeting within the outer medulla. CadN and Sema-1a expression is not affected by dFezf loss, and dFezf loss does not affect CadN/Sema-1a function (dendrites are normal in dFezf mutants but not in CadN/Sema-1a mutants).
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C132 provide RNA-seq and morphological evidence that dFezf does not regulate CadN/Sema-1a expression or function. C128 and C134 appropriately conclude parallel function. The evidence clearly distinguishes dFezf function from the CadN/Sema-1a pathway, supporting independent mechanisms for different aspects of targeting.

results.result: dFezf represents a transcriptional module that constructs M3 layer circuitry through both cell-intrinsic mechanisms (promoting L3 targeting to the proximal domain, essential for layer specificity) and cell-extrinsic mechanisms (activating Netrin to regulate R8 layer specificity). Loss of dFezf disrupts synaptic connectivity with Tm9 target cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C22, C26, and C27 summarize the major findings with appropriate support from the detailed experiments. C23 and C28 are reasonable inferences from the data. C29 appropriately synthesizes the findings into a coherent model. The dual cell-intrinsic and cell-extrinsic functions are well-demonstrated through the combined genetic, expression, and connectivity analyses.

results.result: The use of transcriptional modules like dFezf to coordinate neural connections within correct layers through cell-intrinsic and cell-extrinsic mechanisms may represent a conserved strategy for building laminar-specific circuits, with potential parallels in mammalian systems including the mouse retina and cerebral cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C30, C124, C125, C136, and C139 are explicitly speculative proposals about conservation and generality. While C135, C137, and C138 provide supporting citations for Fezf expression and function in mammalian systems, direct functional evidence for analogous dual mechanisms is lacking. The proposal is reasonable and well-motivated but requires experimental validation in other systems.

results.result: Some L3-specific genes are downregulated and genes expressed in other lamina neurons become upregulated in dFezf mutant L3 neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44 reference RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript showing bidirectional expression changes. While specific genes are not detailed in these claims, the general pattern is consistent with the comprehensive RNA-seq analysis (C76-C78) and supports partial changes in gene expression programs without complete cell fate transformation.

results.result: dFezf is cell-autonomously required for targeting L3 growth cones to the proximal domain of the outer medulla, which may be necessary for subsequent segregation into the developing M3 layer.
results.evaluation: C58 is well-supported by the MARCM and rescue experiments. C59 is appropriately speculative ('may be necessary') as the direct link between broad domain targeting and layer segregation is inferred from the developmental sequence rather than directly tested. The speculation is reasonable but would require additional experiments to definitively establish causality.
